name: Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemicord)
presentation: After a stab wound to the back, or with a lateral disc or tumor pressing on one side of the cord, a patient has weakness of the leg on one side with brisk reflexes and an upgoing toe, cannot feel a tuning fork or joint movement in that same leg, yet reports that pin-prick and cold are lost in the other leg, starting a couple of segments below the injury. At the level of the lesion itself there is a narrow band of complete sensory loss and flaccid weakness on the injured side.

deficits.sign: Spastic weakness with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar (lateral corticospinal tract)
Loss of vibration and position sense (posterior column)

deficits.distribution: from 1–2 segments below the lesion downward
deficits.sign: Loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract)

deficits.distribution: at the level of the lesion
deficits.sign: Segmental lower motor neuron weakness and a band of anesthesia from anterior horn and root damage

reasoning: The three long tracts of the cord cross at different places, and a lesion of one half of the cord separates them. The lateral corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla, so it carries the motor command for the same side of the body, and cutting it produces ipsilateral upper motor neuron weakness below the lesion. The posterior columns carry uncrossed proprioceptive and vibration fibers, which cross only in the medulla after relaying in the gracile and cuneate nuclei, so their interruption gives ipsilateral loss of those modalities. The spinothalamic tract, by contrast, is formed by second-order fibers that crossed in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments of their entry, so it carries pain and temperature from the opposite side, and its section gives contralateral loss beginning a segment or two below the lesion, where the fibers entering at the lesion level have not yet crossed. Fibers crossing at the level of the lesion are caught on both sides, and the damaged dorsal root and anterior horn add an ipsilateral segmental band of complete sensory loss and flaccid weakness that marks the level exactly. Light touch survives on both sides because it travels by both routes. The dissociation, with weakness and proprioceptive loss on one side and pain loss on the other, is unique to the cord and cannot be produced by any brain lesion.

imagingFindings.finding: Hemicord signal change and hemorrhage at the level of the wound on T2 and gradient echo; CT for bone and metal fragments.
Lateral disc herniation, meningioma or schwannoma indenting one side of the cord with cord signal change.
Short, eccentric dorsolateral T2 lesion typical of multiple sclerosis, enhancing when acute.

commonCauses: Lateral cervical disc herniation or spondylosis

mimics.name: Lateral medullary syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Facial sensory loss and cranial nerve signs; no limb weakness

mimics.name: Peripheral nerve or plexus injury
mimics.howToDistinguish: Lower motor neuron pattern, no contralateral sensory loss, no level

mimics.name: Conversion disorder
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensory loss splits the midline exactly in all modalities and does not follow tract anatomy

management: Spinal immobilization and urgent MRI when traumatic or compressive; surgical decompression as indicated
Methylprednisolone is not routinely used for traumatic cord injury
Prognosis for walking is the best of the incomplete cord syndromes

imagingHint.label: one half of the cervical cord

examSequence: Find the motor level: last normal muscle group
Pin-prick from the feet upward on each side separately: the level will differ by side
Vibration and joint position in each foot
Look for the narrow band of complete loss at the lesion
